paragraphs: The rain fell in relentless sheets against the stained-glass windows of Harrington Manor, each drop seeming to hammer a nail into the coffin of the evening. Inside the cavernous library, Detective Miles Corbin surveyed the scene with a practiced, weary eye. Lord Alistair Harrington, a man whose wealth was matched only by his list of enemies, was slumped in his favorite wingback chair, an untouched glass of amber liquid on the table beside him. There were no visible wounds, no signs of a struggle; to the casual observer, the old man could have simply drifted off into his final sleep, a peaceful end he had done little in life to deserve.

Standing by the grand fireplace, a nervous young man twisted a signet ring on his finger. This was Arthur Harrington, the deceased's nephew and sole heir, a man who seemed to wear his anxiety like a poorly fitted suit. "I came in to say goodnight, Detective," he stammered, his eyes darting from Corbin to the still figure in the chair. "He was just... sitting there. He hadn't even touched his nightly whiskey. I thought he was sleeping, but he was cold."

A figure appeared in the doorway, framed by the dim hall light, her silhouette sharp and elegant. Clad in a silk dressing gown the color of blood, Eleanor Harrington, Lord Alistair's wife of five years and thirty years his junior, surveyed the room. Her gaze, however, was as cold and hard as the marble mantelpiece; there were no tears, only a flicker of something unreadable before it was replaced by a mask of detached curiosity. "So, the old dragon finally breathed his last," she stated, her voice a low, smooth melody that held no trace of grief.

Corbin's gaze shifted to the untouched drink. "Did he always have a nightcap?" he asked, his voice low and even. Before Arthur or Eleanor could answer, a fourth voice, crisp and formal, answered from the hallway. Jennings, the butler, stood there, his posture as starched as his collar, his face a mask of professional solemnity. "Every evening at precisely nine o'clock, Detective. I poured it for him myself not thirty minutes before Mr. Arthur found him." His eyes flickered towards Eleanor for a fraction of a second, a silent, almost imperceptible exchange that Corbin duly noted.

Corbin moved closer to the wingback chair, his polished shoes silent on the thick Persian rug. He crouched beside the body, ignoring the three pairs of eyes fixed on his back. Leaning in, he detected a faint, unfamiliar scent clinging to the lapel of Lord Harrington's velvet smoking jacket. It was not the usual masculine blend of pipe tobacco and old leather, but something delicate and floral. His gaze lifted from the deceased and drifted across the room, settling on Eleanor. The cloying sweetness of gardenia seemed to emanate from her very presence, a fragrant ghost lingering in the air.

"Lady Harrington," Corbin began, his tone deceptively casual as he rose to his full height, "your perfume is quite distinctive. Gardenia, is it not?" Eleanor met his gaze without flinching, a small, almost mocking smile playing on her lips. "It is. A custom blend. Alistair claimed he adored it, though I suspect he merely tolerated it to keep the peace. Fragrances gave him terrible headaches." She gestured vaguely towards the decanter on the sideboard. "Hence his nightly dose of whiskey – his 'medicine,' as he called it."

Corbin’s eyes narrowed slightly at her casual dismissal. He turned his attention back to the immediate vicinity of the chair, his gaze sweeping the floor with meticulous care. A faint glint of light from beneath the heavy velvet ottoman caught his eye. He crouched, pulling a small evidence envelope from his coat pocket, and carefully nudged the object into view with the tip of a pen. It was a pearl earring, its silver clasp broken. Arthur gasped, his face paling further. "That's Eleanor's. I recognize it. A gift from Uncle Alistair."

All eyes swung to Eleanor. Her painted red lips tightened into a thin line, but her composure remained unshaken. She glided forward, peering down at the small piece of jewelry with an air of mild annoyance. "Yes, that's mine. Or rather, it was," she said, her voice dripping with disdain. "Alistair and I had a... disagreement earlier this evening. He had a tendency to grab when he was trying to make a point. He tore it from my ear. I was so furious I didn't even bother to look for it."

"A disagreement?" Corbin prompted, his voice a silken thread of inquiry. Eleanor sighed, a theatrical display of exasperation. "The same old argument, Detective. Money. He accused me of being a spendthrift, of draining his coffers for my 'frivolous' pursuits. He threatened to cut me off, to amend his will in favor of his precious nephew." She shot a venomous glance at Arthur, who flinched as if struck. "It was nothing new. Empty threats from a bitter old man who knew his power was slipping away."

Corbin let the silence hang in the air for a moment before turning to the butler. "Jennings, you said you prepared the drink. Did you see Lady Harrington near this room after her argument with her husband?" The butler’s gaze was steady, his expression impassive. "I did not, sir. After delivering the whiskey, I retired to the kitchens to oversee the preparations for tomorrow's breakfast. I heard nothing more until Mr. Arthur's cry for help." His answer was too quick, too polished, as if rehearsed.

"And you, Mr. Harrington?" Corbin pivoted to face the jittery nephew. "Where were you during this supposed argument?" Arthur swallowed hard, his Adam's apple bobbing. "I was in my own rooms, in the east wing. I... I could hear their raised voices, even from there. It was quite a nasty row. I didn't want to get involved, so I stayed put until things quieted down. That was about... forty minutes ago, I'd say. I waited a bit before coming down to check on Uncle Alistair."

Corbin paced slowly before the fireplace, his mind weaving together the threads of the evening. An argument over money, a threat to change the will, an earring torn from a lobe in anger. Eleanor had the motive and, it seemed, the opportunity. She was in the room, her scent lingering on the victim, her jewelry discarded in a struggle. Her cold demeanor did her no favors, painting the picture of a ruthless gold-digger who had finally cashed in her most valuable asset. The pieces were fitting together with an almost suspicious neatness.

The medical examiner arrived, a bustling, no-nonsense woman named Dr. Evans. After a brief but thorough examination, she confirmed Corbin's initial assessment. "No obvious cause of death. No marks, no contusions, save for a slight scratch on his hand. Given the circumstances and his history of heart trouble, it could be a simple coronary. But..." she paused, her brow furrowing, "I'll know for sure once I get him back to the lab. Something feels off. We'll run a full toxicology screen."

Corbin seized on her words. "A scratch on his hand?" He moved back to the body, Dr. Evans pointing to a small, angry red line across the back of Lord Harrington's right hand. It looked fresh. "Could have happened during the argument," Corbin mused aloud, his gaze flicking to Eleanor's perfectly manicured nails. "A wife fighting back, perhaps?" Eleanor simply raised a single, elegant eyebrow in response, offering no denial.

Hours later, with the body removed and the manor staff questioned, Corbin found himself back in the library. The room felt emptier now, colder. He walked over to the drinks trolley where the decanter of whiskey stood. Beside it was a small, ornate box, its lid slightly ajar. He opened it. Inside, nestled on a bed of velvet, was a collection of sugar cubes. Nothing unusual, except for one small detail. On the very top, one of the cubes had a tiny, almost invisible speck of greenish-brown powder clinging to its crystalline surface.

His thoughts immediately turned to poison. A substance introduced into the nightly whiskey. He carefully bagged the sugar cube, his mind racing. Who had access to this room, to the drinks trolley? All three of them, of course. Yet his mind kept circling back to Eleanor. Her argument with Alistair provided the classic motive. A scorned wife, about to be disinherited, decides to take matters into her own hands. A quiet poison, slipped into his drink, would look just like the heart attack everyone expected the old man to have eventually.

The following morning, Corbin received a preliminary report from Dr. Evans. "You were right to be suspicious, Miles," her voice crackled over the phone. "His blood is full of digitalis. An extract from the foxglove plant. A high enough dose would induce cardiac arrest, mimicking a heart attack almost perfectly." Corbin felt a grim satisfaction. "And the scratch on his hand?" he asked. "Defensive wound," she confirmed. "The skin under his own fingernails has traces of someone else's DNA. Also, traces of a fragrant hand cream. Gardenia, to be exact."

The pieces clicked into place with a definitive snap. The gardenia scent on the body, the earring, the argument, the financial motive, and now, the gardenia-scented hand cream under the victim's fingernails from a defensive scratch. Eleanor Harrington was the clear culprit. Corbin called for a uniformed officer to meet him at the manor. He would have the pleasure of seeing that cool, arrogant mask of hers finally crack. He was confident, certain. The case was all but closed.

Corbin arrived back at Harrington Manor, the early morning sun doing little to dispel the gloom that clung to the old house. He found Eleanor in the conservatory, calmly sipping tea and reading a book as if nothing had happened. "Lady Harrington," he announced, his voice ringing with authority, "I'm placing you under arrest for the murder of your husband, Lord Alistair Harrington." He laid out the evidence: the poison, the motive, the earring, and the final, damning clue of the gardenia-scented cream found under Alistair's fingernails.

For the first time, Eleanor's composure faltered. A look of genuine shock, not of fear or guilt, flashed across her face. "Gardenia hand cream?" she repeated, her voice incredulous. "Detective, you are mistaken. I can't stand the stuff. My perfume is one thing, but I would never use a cream in that scent. It's far too overpowering. The only person in this house who uses gardenia-scented hand cream is Arthur."

The detective froze, Eleanor's words hanging in the air like a discordant note. He replayed the evening in his mind, every detail, every glance. He had been so focused on Eleanor, on the obvious trail she left. The perfume. The earring. He had seen Arthur as weak, nervous, a pawn in the drama. But now, he remembered the young man's hands, constantly fidgeting, twisting that ring. He remembered the faint scent of flowers he'd initially attributed to Eleanor's overpowering perfume. And he remembered the butler's flicker of a glance—not at Eleanor, but towards the hallway where Arthur had been standing.

"Jennings," Corbin's voice was sharp, cutting through the sudden tension in the room as he summoned the butler, who appeared as if by magic. "Lord Harrington's nightcap. You said you poured it. Who was with you?" Jennings's professional facade finally crumbled, his shoulders slumping in defeat. "Mr. Arthur, sir. He came into the pantry as I was preparing the tray. Said he wanted to take it to his uncle himself, as a... a peace offering after the terrible row with Lady Harrington. He offered to add the sugar cube, as his uncle preferred."

Suddenly, Arthur’s anxiety made perfect sense. It wasn’t the nervousness of an innocent bystander; it was the frantic energy of a killer watching his carefully constructed plan fall apart. He had used Eleanor’s very public and very loud argument with Alistair as the perfect cover. He had counted on everyone suspecting the volatile young wife. He likely planted the earring he'd found after their fight, a piece of manufactured evidence to seal her fate. The perfume that clung to Alistair wasn't from a close embrace, but from Arthur himself, who had been doused in his aunt's signature scent after she stormed past him in the hall following the argument.

Corbin confronted Arthur in the library, the scene of the crime. The young man's composure shattered under the weight of the new accusations. He confessed it all, his words tumbling out in a torrent of resentment and greed. His uncle had been planning to write him out of the will after all, not because of Eleanor, but because of Arthur's mounting gambling debts. The "peace offering" was a poisoned sugar cube, laced with a digitalis concoction he'd cultivated from the foxgloves in the manor's own garden. When Alistair had realized something was wrong, that the whiskey tasted bitter, he had reached out, scratching Arthur's hand—the hand covered in the incriminating gardenia cream—in a last, desperate act.

As the uniformed officers led a sobbing Arthur Harrington away, Corbin stood by the window, watching the rain begin to fall once more. Eleanor stood in the doorway, her silk robe now looking less like a symbol of cold indifference and more like armor. "He used my histrionics to his advantage," she said quietly, her voice devoid of its earlier mockery. "He knew everyone would see the greedy young wife, not the desperate nephew." Corbin nodded, the misleading clues—the scent, the earring, the argument—now rearranged in his mind, forming a picture that was not only different, but terrifyingly clear. The most obvious suspect had been nothing more than a perfectly crafted distraction.
